clue.text: Send off old wine

blocks.note: ex- means former, as in an ex-husband
port is a fortified wine from Portugal

explanation.surface: Someone getting rid of a bottle of wine that has gone past its best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send off' reads like dismissing the wine, but it is the whole definition; 'old wine' splits into a prefix and a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To export goods is to ship them abroad for sale, a fair synonym for dispatching them.

clue.text: Romeo forced out and cast aside

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
thrown out by force, as from a club or a pilot's seat

explanation.surface: Romeo, banished from Verona and abandoned, as in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Shakespeare's banished lover, but Romeo is just the radio-alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rejected has been refused and thrown away, the same as being discarded or cast aside.

clue.text: Dig starters of parsnip, liver and octopus — yuck!

indicators.note: a starter is the first course, so only the opening letter of each following word is served up

blocks.note: the first letters of the three foods
an exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: A diner faced with a starter of parsnip, liver and octopus is understandably disgusted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starters' looks like a menu course, but it means first letters; 'and' sits inside the fodder list and gives nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To plough a field is to turn over the soil, a farming sense of digging the ground.

clue.text: Nation's wicked slandering — no sir!

indicators.note: saying no to something refuses it entry, so those letters are struck out of the fodder
wicked means wrong or bad, so the letters are behaving badly and land in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then removed letter by letter

explanation.surface: A politician protests that the country's spiteful slanders are untrue: no, sir!
explanation.walkthrough: Take S, I and R out of SLANDERING to leave LANDENG, then rearrange. 'No sir!' reads as an indignant denial, not a removal.
explanation.definitionFit: England is a country within the United Kingdom, an example of a nation.

clue.text: Article abolishing right of secular organisation

indicators.note: to abolish something is to do away with it, so a letter is removed
organising things means arranging them, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper article about a secular body that does away with someone's rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organisation' reads as a noun, a secular group, but it signals rearranging the six letters left once R goes.
explanation.definitionFit: In a contract or treaty, an article is a numbered section or provision, another name for a clause.

clue.text: Finish close second in race

indicators.note: second points at position two in the word before it, so only that one letter is kept
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the second letter of the word
to race is to compete

explanation.surface: A runner finishes a close second in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close second' looks like a narrow runner-up, but 'second' picks the second letter of 'close', which then goes inside the verb for racing.
explanation.definitionFit: To complete a task is to bring it to an end, so the verb matches finish.

clue.text: Spreadsheet: advanced and superb

blocks.note: Microsoft's well-known spreadsheet program
to advance money is to lend it, so advanced can mean lent

explanation.surface: A review praising a spreadsheet as advanced and superb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advanced' reads as sophisticated, describing the software, but it means lent, as in advancing someone a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are adjectives of high praise for something outstanding and of the very best quality.

clue.text: Look into Mafia to come back and thrive

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way it came, so the word is read in the other direction
going into something puts it inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: lo is an old word meaning look, as in 'lo and behold'
the Mob is a common name for the Mafia

explanation.surface: A detective investigating the Mafia expects it to return and prosper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look into' sounds like investigating, but it is the short word for look going into the gang name turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants and people that bloom are flourishing or doing well, a figurative synonym for thriving.

clue.text: Toy filled with wrong fuel, sadly

indicators.note: something filled has its contents inside it, so one piece goes within the other
letters put in wrongly are in the wrong order, so they need rearranging

blocks.note: a dolly is a child's doll
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A sad tale of a toy car filled up with the wrong fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a misfuelled car, but the toy is a doll, and 'wrong' scrambles the fuel before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolefully describes acting in a mournful, sorrowful manner, so both adverbs express unhappiness.

clue.text: Politician covered in sauce rises suddenly

indicators.note: something covered in a coating is wrapped inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: MP is Member of Parliament
jus is a thin gravy or meat juice used as a sauce

explanation.surface: A politician doused in sauce leaps up in shock.
explanation.walkthrough: JUS is the French cooking term for a thin sauce of meat juices, common on British menus.
explanation.definitionFit: When a price jumps it shoots up abruptly, so the verb means rising all at once.

clue.text: Give out when time's up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the word is turned around

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something packs up and stops working once its time is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give out' and 'time's up' both sound like something expiring, but the phrase means release, and 'up' turns the word over in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit light or heat is to send it out or release it, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Small, small person may be cross

definitions.note: cross is not a synonym but an example: cross-stitch is one kind, and 'may be' signals the example

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
titch is British slang for a very small person

explanation.surface: A little person may well get angry about being called small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as angry, but it is the cross-stitch of embroidery. Titch is British slang for a tiny person.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross-stitch is a common embroidery technique, so a cross is one particular type of needlework loop.

clue.text: Came to sorry end, swallowing pigment

indicators.note: something in a sorry state is a mess, so these letters are jumbled
to swallow is to take inside, so one piece ends up within the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
umber is a brown earth pigment used in paints

explanation.surface: Someone who met a miserable fate after eating paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came to sorry end' reads as dying badly, but 'came to' is the definition, in the sense of totalling.
explanation.definitionFit: A crowd that numbered a thousand came to a thousand: both mean amounted to a total.

clue.text: Impressed? Not me! Rubbish web designers

indicators.note: not having something means it is absent, so those letters are left out
rubbish is trash, so the remaining letters are thrown about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: A critic sneers at the work of some website designers: not impressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop M and E from IMPRESSED and rearrange the rest. 'Web designers' sounds like people building websites; it means creatures that spin webs.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiders literally design and build webs, a witty literal reading of a job title.

clue.text: Thought supreme deity initially mad

indicators.note: something mad is crazy and out of order, so these letters are scrambled
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A sceptic suspects the supreme god was out of his mind from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' sits after the fodder and scrambles it; 'initially' picks the first letter of the god.
explanation.definitionFit: If you presumed something you supposed or assumed it, so the past tense matches thought.

clue.text: Some offer a reward — definitely not well done!

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters are found within

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the end of the first word, the middle word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A disappointed winner says the prize offered was poor, hardly a well-done job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well done' looks like praise, but it is how steak is cooked; the opposite of well done is barely cooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare steak is cooked only briefly, the opposite end of the scale from meat cooked through.

clue.text: Determined individual finally loses heart

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the last letter of the word
ticker is informal slang for the heart

explanation.surface: A resolute person who at last becomes discouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loses heart' reads as despairing, but 'loses' only gives its end letter and the heart is the ticker.
explanation.definitionFit: A sticker is someone who sticks at things and perseveres, a dogged or persistent person.

clue.text: Proves company is involved in fraudulent activities

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: cons are swindles or confidence tricks
a firm is a business

explanation.surface: An investigation proves a company has been mixed up in fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: The swindles split around the business, and 'is' just links the two parts of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm a claim is to establish it as true, verifying it just as proving does.

clue.text: Get on with five in a whirl?

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, so a piece goes within the next

blocks.note: taken as written
a whirl is a spin round, like a dance
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: A dizzy question: can you cope with five things spinning at once?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on with' sounds like getting along with someone, but 'Get on' means make progress; the Roman five sits inside 'a dance'.
explanation.definitionFit: To advance is to move forward or make progress, which is what getting on means.

clue.text: Needed some paper in colour

indicators.note: being in something puts it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: red is a colour
a quire is a set quantity of paper, 24 or 25 sheets

explanation.surface: An artist who needed coloured paper for a project.
explanation.walkthrough: A quire is an old trade measure of paper sheets, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Something required was needed or necessary, so the past participles match exactly.

clue.text: How's your father upholding higher education for all?

indicators.note: to uphold is to hold up from beneath, so in a down entry the first piece sits underneath

blocks.note: uni is short for university
a jokey British euphemism for sexual activity

explanation.surface: Someone's dad supports making university open to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: "How's your father" looks like a polite enquiry; it is old British music-hall slang for sex, and it holds up the university from below.
explanation.definitionFit: Unisex clothing or toilets are designed for both men and women, so suitable for everyone.

clue.text: Make a friendly gesture, we're told, to obtain pet

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the letters follow the sound

blocks.note: to win a prize is to obtain it
a cat is a common pet; heard after the first word, its hard C sound joins the end of that word

explanation.surface: Advice on making friends with a pet: be friendly to win it over.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'win cat' quickly and the K sound slides back onto the first word, giving a flirtatious eye gesture plus 'at'.
explanation.definitionFit: Winking at someone is a playful signal of friendliness or complicity, a gesture made with one eye.

clue.text: Wreak havoc over drug being less potent

indicators.note: havoc is chaos and destruction, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
E is short for ecstasy

explanation.surface: A drug causing chaos even though it has been diluted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wreak havoc' is a set phrase, so 'havoc' hides as part of it while signalling the rearrangement of the first word plus the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: A weaker medicine has lower strength or effect, the comparative of feeble meaning less strong.

clue.text: Very little money provided by New York to support a writer

indicators.note: supporting means holding up from beneath, so in a down entry the earlier piece goes underneath

blocks.note: taken as written
a pen is a writing instrument
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A struggling author living on a pittance from New York patrons.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer looks like an author, but it is the pen; New York sits beneath it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A penny is a coin of the lowest value, so the phrase stands for a trivial sum.

clue.text: This could be the apple of the teacher's eye?

definitions.text: This could be the apple of the teacher's eye?

blocks.clueFragment: the apple of the teacher's eye
blocks.note: surface reading: a favourite student, the one the teacher dotes on
setter's reading: the 'apple' of an eye is an old name for the dark centre of the eyeball

explanation.surface: A teacher's favourite in the class.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer works both ways: a schoolchild who is the teacher's favourite, and the opening in the centre of the teacher's eye, once called its apple.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a student at school and the dark circular aperture in the iris.

clue.text: Mother looks over home publications

indicators.note: to look over something is to cover it from above, so one piece is spread round the other

blocks.note: an informal word for mother
a gaze is a long look
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: Mum flicking through home décor glossies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks over' reads as browsing, but 'over' wraps the looks around the word for home.
explanation.definitionFit: Magazines are periodicals, a specific type of printed publication issued regularly.

clue.text: Not as many women get into free running

indicators.note: getting into something means entering it, so one piece goes inside another
running suggests movement, so these letters are on the move into a new order

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for women, as on toilet doors
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that fewer women take up free running, the urban sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free running' is the urban sport parkour, but here 'running' scrambles 'free' around the women's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Fewer is the comparative used for countable things, meaning a smaller number of them.

clue.text: Highly obvious to vocalise about pick of the bunch

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps itself around the other

blocks.note: to vocalise is to use the voice, as in singing
the cream is the best part, the elite

explanation.surface: A singer's talent was glaring enough to be voiced over the best of the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick of the bunch' looks like choosing, but it is a noun phrase for the best, which the verb for vocalising wraps.
explanation.definitionFit: A screaming error is glaringly conspicuous, so the adjective means blatantly evident or unmistakable.
